title: Putting savings inside an e-wallet did not make it feel like savings

children.text: The product made a savings account easier to access from AstraPay. The harder question was how people would understand the money once it appeared inside an e-wallet.
In research, the existing wallet balance already had a clear role. People treated it as money that was ready to spend on everyday transactions.

A savings product placed too close to that balance could easily be read as the same wallet with a better return. That would make the product easier to access, but not necessarily easier to understand.

callout: The product needed enough separation to feel different from spending money without pretending to be a complete saving system.

title: Inspect the evidence behind the positioning
description: The research looked at how people interpreted wallet money, what made savings feel more real, and how similar products were positioned elsewhere.

tabs.label: Wallet mental model
tabs.title: Wallet balance was still spending money
tabs.description: The existing e-wallet context shaped how any new balance would be interpreted before users read product copy.
tabs.alt: Research synthesis about how users perceive e-wallet balance
tabs.caption: The starting point was the mental model users already brought into AstraPay.

tabs.label: Saving cues
tabs.title: Separation made saving feel more intentional
tabs.description: A different name, balance, hierarchy, or usage rule could help users read the money as something set aside rather than immediately spendable.
tabs.alt: Research synthesis about cues that make money feel like savings
tabs.caption: The word savings alone was not enough to create a separate mental account.

tabs.label: Competitor benchmark
tabs.title: Adoption was often driven by practical value
tabs.description: Similar products were not adopted only because users wanted to save. Convenience, activation, promotions, and ecosystem integration also mattered.
tabs.alt: Competitor benchmark for savings products connected to digital wallets
tabs.caption: The product story needed to work for everyday money management, not just saving intent.

title: Too close to the wallet and the product loses its purpose
description: The interface and brand needed to show that the money served a different purpose even though it remained accessible from the same ecosystem.

left.label: Too integrated
left.title: It reads like a wallet with perks
left.description: If the new balance looks and behaves like the main wallet, interest or other benefits can feel like an add-on to spending money.
left.note: Easy to understand operationally, weak as a separate financial proposition.

right.label: Clear separation
right.title: It feels like money with another purpose
right.description: A distinct balance, naming system, and visual hierarchy can make the product feel separate while keeping access simple from AstraPay.
right.note: The separation needs to come from the product structure, not copy alone.

title: We also had to avoid promising a saving experience that did not exist yet

children.text: The product did not yet include tools such as saving goals, automated saving, budgeting, or deeper money-management features. A strong saving claim could create expectations that the experience could not support.
I pushed for a position that made the balance clearly different from everyday wallet money while staying grounded in what the product could actually do.

The benchmark also helped here. Practical value such as easy activation and integration with existing transactions could support adoption without turning every message into a promise about becoming a better saver.

title: Research became four working principles
description: These principles were used in product and branding discussions with the partner team.

metrics.label: Give the balance its own identity
metrics.context: Different enough from everyday wallet money

metrics.label: Keep access familiar
metrics.context: Still clearly part of the AstraPay ecosystem

metrics.label: Do not overclaim saving
metrics.context: Match the promise to current product capability

metrics.label: Show the hierarchy in the interface
metrics.context: Do not rely on naming and copy alone

title: The distinction had to survive even when users ignored the copy
description: Naming could explain the relationship, but the product still needed to look different at a glance.

left.label: Copy-led
left.title: Explain that this is a savings product
left.description: Useful for onboarding and education, but fragile if the two balances still look like one pool of money.
left.note: Understanding depends too heavily on users reading.

right.label: Structure-led
right.title: Make the distinction visible before explanation
right.description: Balance hierarchy, naming, and product identity work together so users can tell wallet money from the linked savings balance.
right.note: Copy then explains a distinction the interface already makes visible.

title: The branding discussion started from the product position

children.text: I brought the research and competitor findings into a joint workshop with the partner team. The discussion focused on how AstraPay, the partner brand, and the product name should relate inside one experience.

We used the positioning to evaluate branding hierarchy and visual directions. A logo direction only made sense if it helped the product feel distinct without disconnecting it from the two brands behind it.
The shortlisted directions then moved into partner and leadership review with a clearer reason for why the product should look the way it did.

callout: The workshop was not a logo exercise first. The visual direction had to support a product position we could defend.

title: The research gave the product a clearer place inside AstraPay

children.text: The work established a clearer direction for how the linked savings product should appear alongside the main wallet. It needed its own identity and hierarchy because the two balances served different purposes.
It also set a boundary for the product story. We could communicate financial value and convenience without implying that the current experience already provided a full set of saving tools.
Those findings became input for product framing, branding architecture, and the visual directions taken into the next review rounds.
